promptText: What does the dot product between two embedding vectors intuitively measure?
options: How many words the two underlying pieces of text share
How much the two vectors point in the same direction, weighted by how long they both are
The total number of dimensions in each vector
Whether the two vectors were produced by the same embedding model
explanation: The dot product multiplies corresponding components and sums them; vectors pointing in similar directions produce a large positive sum, unrelated (perpendicular) directions produce a sum near zero, and opposite directions produce a large negative sum -- it captures directional agreement scaled by magnitude.

promptText: What does it mean to 'normalize' an embedding vector?
options: Rounding every component to the nearest integer
Rescaling the vector so its magnitude (length) becomes exactly 1, while preserving its direction
Sorting the vector's components from largest to smallest
Converting the vector from float32 to float64 precision
explanation: Normalizing divides every component by the vector's own magnitude, producing a unit-length vector pointing in the same direction; this is done so that a cheap dot product becomes mathematically identical to cosine similarity.

promptText: Why is cosine similarity generally preferred over raw dot product or Euclidean distance for comparing text embeddings?
options: Cosine similarity is always faster to compute than any other metric
Cosine similarity measures only the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude, so incidental differences in vector length don't distort the similarity ranking
Cosine similarity is the only metric that works on vectors with more than 100 dimensions
Cosine similarity always produces positive numbers, making it easier to threshold
explanation: Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both vectors' magnitudes, leaving a pure measure of orientation; this matters because raw dot product or Euclidean distance can be dominated by incidental magnitude differences (e.g., longer text chunks producing larger-magnitude embeddings) rather than actual meaning.

promptText: What is Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) search, and why is it used instead of brute-force search at scale?
options: ANN search only works for embeddings with fewer than 100 dimensions
ANN search uses an index built ahead of time to skip comparing against most stored vectors, trading a small amount of recall for dramatically lower query latency at large collection sizes
ANN search guarantees perfectly correct top-k results while running faster than brute-force through better hardware alone
ANN search eliminates the need to choose a distance metric entirely
explanation: Brute-force search compares a query against every stored vector, scaling linearly with collection size; ANN algorithms like HNSW and IVF exploit geometric structure to prune most candidates, accepting a probabilistic (not guaranteed) recall in exchange for large speed gains.

promptText: For two unit-normalized vectors (magnitude exactly 1), what is the relationship between their dot product and their cosine similarity?
options: They are unrelated and must be computed independently
They are exactly equal, because dividing by magnitudes of 1 leaves the cosine similarity formula equal to the raw dot product
The dot product is always double the cosine similarity
Cosine similarity can only be computed after first computing the Euclidean distance
explanation: Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the product of the two magnitudes; when both magnitudes equal 1, the denominator collapses to 1, so cosine similarity and the raw dot product become numerically identical -- the basis for why production systems normalize vectors at write time.

promptText: What does HNSW stand for, and what is the basic intuition behind its search strategy?
options: Hierarchical Navigable Small World -- a graph-based index where search starts at a sparse top layer for large geometric hops, then descends to denser layers for precise local refinement
High-dimensional Numerical Similarity Weighting -- a formula for combining cosine similarity and Euclidean distance
Hashed Nearest Search Window -- a technique for hashing vectors into fixed-size buckets
Horizontal Node Sharding Workflow -- a method for distributing an index across servers
explanation: HNSW builds a multi-layer graph where sparse upper layers allow large jumps across the space cheaply, and the search progressively descends to denser layers for fine-grained neighbor refinement, analogous to using highways before local streets.

promptText: A vector index is configured with Euclidean distance, but the embedding model was trained and evaluated exclusively using cosine similarity. Why does this produce silently degraded results rather than an obvious error?
options: The vector database will refuse to run any query with a mismatched metric, so this scenario cannot actually occur

Euclidean distance measures something the model never optimized for (it factors in magnitude, which the training objective ignored), so queries still execute and return plausible-looking ranked results, just systematically wrong ones with no exception thrown
Euclidean distance is mathematically identical to cosine similarity for all vectors, so there is no actual problem
The embedding model automatically converts its output to match whatever metric the index is configured with
explanation: A distance function computes a numeric result for any pair of same-dimension vectors regardless of whether the result is semantically meaningful; since the model was trained to place related items at a small angle (not a small absolute distance), using Euclidean distance measures something the model never optimized for, degrading quality without raising any error.

promptText: In an IVF (Inverted File) index, what does increasing the nprobe parameter do?
options: It increases the number of dimensions used per vector, improving precision at the cost of storage

It increases how many of the nearest clusters (Voronoi cells) a query searches inside instead of just the single closest one, improving recall for queries near cluster boundaries at the cost of higher latency
It increases the number of centroids used to partition the entire collection during index construction
It converts the index from approximate to guaranteed-exact search
explanation: Searching only the single nearest cluster risks missing a true nearest neighbor sitting just across a Voronoi cell boundary; increasing nprobe examines more nearby clusters, directly trading additional query latency for improved recall on boundary cases.

promptText: Why can cosine similarity and Euclidean distance rank two candidate vectors differently against the same query, when vectors are not normalized?
options: Cosine similarity only measures angle (ignoring magnitude), while Euclidean distance is sensitive to both angle and magnitude, so a long vector pointing in a slightly different direction can be favored by one metric and disfavored by the other
Cosine similarity and Euclidean distance always produce identical rankings regardless of normalization
Euclidean distance cannot be computed on vectors with more than 3 dimensions
Cosine similarity is only defined for integer-valued vectors
explanation: A short vector pointing almost exactly toward the query can score highest on cosine similarity (small angle) while a long vector at a bigger angle can score closest on Euclidean distance if its raw endpoint happens to sit nearer -- the two metrics are only guaranteed to agree when all vectors are unit-normalized.

promptText: What does 'recall@k' measure when evaluating an Approximate Nearest Neighbor index?
options: The percentage of queries that return results within the required latency budget
The fraction of the true top-k nearest neighbors (from exact brute-force search) that the approximate index actually returns in its own top-k results
The total number of vectors stored in the index divided by k
The average cosine similarity score of the top-k results, regardless of ground truth
explanation: Recall@k directly quantifies the accuracy price paid for an ANN index's speed: it compares the approximate index's top-k results against the true top-k from exact search, and is tuned via parameters like HNSW's ef_search or IVF's nprobe to trade recall against latency.

promptText: Why does product quantization (PQ) dramatically reduce the memory footprint of a large-scale vector index?
options: It deletes vectors that are judged to be near-duplicates of other stored vectors
It splits each vector into smaller sub-vectors, replaces each sub-vector with the ID of its nearest codebook centroid, and stores only those compact IDs instead of full-precision floats
It reduces every vector to exactly 2 dimensions regardless of the original embedding size
It stores only the average of all vectors in the collection instead of individual vectors
explanation: PQ splits a vector into chunks, learns a small codebook of representative centroids per chunk, and stores just a single-byte codebook ID per chunk instead of the full floating-point sub-vector, achieving large compression ratios at the cost of representing each vector only approximately.

promptText: A team notices cosine similarity scores between queries and retrieved documents all cluster tightly in a narrow range (e.g., 0.78-0.84), regardless of actual relevance. What does this most likely indicate, and what is the correct response?
options: The vector database is broken and must be reinstalled

This is a classic symptom of anisotropic embedding geometry compressing the achievable score range; the fix is to calibrate similarity thresholds empirically per model using known-related and known-unrelated pairs rather than trusting a fixed absolute cutoff
The embedding model has stopped working and must be retrained from scratch
This always means the vectors were not normalized and must be re-embedded immediately
explanation: Many embedding models occupy a narrow cone of the full space (anisotropy), compressing scores into a tight range; absolute similarity thresholds are model- and corpus-specific and must be empirically calibrated with a labeled set, rather than assumed universal (e.g., '0.8 means very similar').

promptText: A vector search system shows excellent recall@k in offline evaluation, but users report noticeably worse real-world search quality. What is the most likely class of explanation, and how should it be investigated first?
options: The ANN index parameters must be retuned to higher ef_search or nprobe values without further investigation

The labeled evaluation set or configuration may not represent real production traffic or settings; first confirm the offline eval and production system use identical index parameters, embedding model version, and distance metric before assuming the search algorithm itself is at fault
This gap is impossible; if offline recall@k is high, production quality must also be high
The only possible cause is that the vector database vendor's software has a bug
explanation: A gap between offline metrics and real-world quality is very often a methodology gap -- evaluation-set drift, a config mismatch between offline eval and production, or metrics that don't capture what users actually experience (like ranking order within top-k) -- so confirming configuration parity is the correct first diagnostic step before re-tuning the algorithm.

promptText: Why does the algebraic identity ||A-B||^2 = ||A||^2 - 2(A·B) + ||B||^2 matter computationally when comparing a query against a large batch of stored vectors?
options: It proves that Euclidean distance and cosine similarity are always identical for any pair of vectors

It allows ||A||^2 and ||B||^2 to be precomputed once and cached, leaving only the cross term A·B (computable efficiently via matrix multiplication) to be freshly calculated per comparison, avoiding a full subtract-square-sum loop for every pair
It eliminates the need to ever compute a dot product
It guarantees that Euclidean distance will always be smaller than the dot product
explanation: Since ||A||^2 (for stored vectors, at index-build time) and ||B||^2 (for the query, once per query) can be precomputed, batch squared Euclidean distances reduce to one efficient matrix multiplication for the cross terms plus cheap precomputed offsets, rather than an expensive per-pair loop -- a significant speedup at scale for a mathematically identical result.

promptText: Why is choosing the correct distance metric (matching the embedding model's training objective) fundamentally different, as an engineering decision, from choosing between exact and approximate search?
options: Both decisions are identical trade-offs where a 'wrong' choice still has some compensating benefit

The distance metric choice is a correctness decision with no legitimate trade-off -- a mismatched metric only produces silently worse results with no upside -- whereas exact-vs-approximate is a genuine, tunable trade-off between measurable recall and measurable latency/cost
Distance metric choice only matters for images, while exact-vs-approximate only matters for text
Exact search always uses cosine similarity, while approximate search always uses Euclidean distance
explanation: Picking a distance metric inconsistent with what the embedding model was trained for has no upside -- it just silently degrades quality; by contrast, exact-vs-approximate search is a legitimate curve where both options are 'correct' (use the right metric) but trade recall against latency and cost based on the application's actual constraints.
